evaluation.positioning_hook: A burned-out jazz pianist in Lisbon is offered bunker salvation if he finishes one last song before impact, then falls for a woman who may be his last reason to stay human.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional engine is clear and accessible — love, survival, and a ticking apocalypse — but the script plays in a more adult, prestige lane than broad commercial genre. The audience is real, especially for romance-forward sci-fi drama, yet the long, lyrical scenes and melancholy register narrow the four-quadrant reach.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands immediately: a pianist in a collapsing Lisbon is trading music for bunker access while the world counts down to impact. The opening bar sequence, the watch, the passports, and George's offer establish the engine fast and clean.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Morgan has a strong contradiction — technically gifted, emotionally shut down, and desperate to matter — and Marie gives the story a vivid counterforce. Michel and George are also sharply drawn, though the script is still led by Morgan's interiority more than by a truly ensemble-level character web.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to a jazz-poetic apocalypse, using music, ticking time, and luxury-as-tomb imagery as a unified language. The repeated dream-space asteroid imagery and the bunker-as-curated-mausoleum concept give it a confident, ownable voice.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story has a strong forward engine — passports, the song, George's demands, Marie's choice — and the pressure keeps escalating. It does spend real time in mood and repetition, so the propulsion is more elegiac than breakneck, but the act turns are still legible and motivated.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script finds a fresh emotional shape in a familiar end-of-the-world setup by making the central conflict about art, preservation, and what deserves to survive. Morgan's song, George's collection, and Marie's refusal to be bought make the premise feel both novel and inevitable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Lisbon hotel ecosystem feels specific and story-generating: the bar economy, the passport black market, the bunker hierarchy, the ruined city outside, and the class divide between George's vault and the street. The world is not just backdrop; it actively shapes every transaction and relationship.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: This has a very distinct tonal signature: apocalyptic but intimate, romantic but unsentimental, lush but decaying. The jazz language, the ticking motif, and the visual contrast between silk luxury and civic collapse create a hard-to-mistake register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script keeps revealing emotional subtext through objects — the watch, the Polaroid, the unfinished song, the passports — and the asteroid countdown gives every choice a second meaning. There is real depth in the Morgan/Marie/George triangle, even when the surface plot is straightforward.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Morgan/Michel, Morgan/George, and Morgan/Marie all generate distinct energy, and the hotel guests create a living pressure-cooker around them. Still, the script is fundamentally anchored to Morgan, with the supporting players functioning more as vivid mirrors and catalysts than as a fully modular ensemble.

lead_characters.name: Morgan Aireheart
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s, white/European-presenting, professional musician, emotionally guarded, urban cosmopolitan
lead_characters.hook: A gifted but broken jazz pianist living on borrowed time in Lisbon, Morgan has the posture of a man who has already lost the argument with life. He hides grief behind precision, wears a cracked watch like a talisman, and keeps circling the same unfinished song as if completion might redeem the past. His arc is about whether survival without integrity is actually survival at all.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Oscar Isaac in Inside Llewyn Davis or Ethan Hawke in First Reformed — a wounded, articulate lead whose stillness, musicality, and self-protective cruelty are the performance. It gives an actor a chance to play virtuosity, shame, romantic longing, and a late-film moral reversal in one role.

lead_characters.name: Marie Freeling
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, American, emotionally resilient, working-to-middle class, musical
lead_characters.hook: Marie is the script's living counterargument to Morgan's fatalism: sharp, playful, wounded, and stubbornly unbuyable. She can flirt, needle, sing, and read a room instantly, but beneath the wit is a woman who has already stared down despair and chosen to keep moving. She is not a passive love interest; she is the story's conscience and its most dangerous source of hope.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Saoirse Ronan in Brooklyn or Rebecca Hall in Vicky Cristina Barcelona room to be luminous without being ornamental. It offers an actor a rare blend of romantic chemistry, emotional authority, and a late-film moral stance that changes the story.

lead_characters.name: George
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 60s, affluent, controlled, likely European or transatlantic elite
lead_characters.hook: George is a collector of people disguised as a patron of the arts. He speaks in calm, surgical sentences, treats scarcity like a market, and sees Morgan less as a man than as an asset to be preserved and owned. He is the film's coldest embodiment of survivalism: elegant, rational, and morally dead-eyed.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do Christopher Walken in The Dead Zone or Ralph Fiennes in The Grand Budapest Hotel — elegant menace with a civilized surface and a predator's intelligence underneath. The part offers controlled stillness, verbal precision, and the pleasure of playing power without volume.

lead_characters.name: Michel
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, Portuguese, bartender, observant, emotionally contained
lead_characters.hook: Michel is the hotel's ballast: dry, humane, and quietly philosophical, with the weary competence of someone who has already accepted the end and decided to keep working anyway. He gives the film its grounded moral center, moving bodies, pouring drinks, and delivering the kind of plainspoken wisdom that lands because he never asks to be heard. He is the rare supporting character who feels like he has lived a whole other movie offscreen.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor material in the vein of Richard Jenkins in The Visitor or Barkhad Abdi in Captain Phillips — a role that wins by restraint, dignity, and lived-in authority. It gives an actor the chance to be the emotional anchor without ever becoming sentimental.

lead_characters.name: Ava
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, glamorous, socially agile, likely hotel regular / opportunist
lead_characters.hook: Ava is all surface voltage until the script lets the grief underneath show through. She flirts, bargains, and performs ease in a collapsing world, but her attachment to Markus and her reactions to the violence around her suggest a woman who is improvising survival in real time. She adds volatility and a sense of social predation to the hotel ecosystem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play against type the way Jena Malone did in The Neon Demon or Jennifer Jason Leigh in The Hateful Eight — seductive, brittle, and harder to read than she first appears. The part offers sharp entrances, emotional reversals, and a strong visual signature.

lead_characters.name: Markus
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s, unstable, addicted/medically dependent, socially compromised
lead_characters.hook: Markus is a charming liability: needy, impulsive, and already half-lost before the story starts. His insulin dependence and his connection to the passport scheme make him both vulnerable and dangerous, and his death becomes the plot's first major moral rupture. He functions as the human cost of the bunker economy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but memorable role that gives an actor a volatile, tragic burst in the mold of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Ben Foster in Hell or High Water. It offers intensity, fragility, and a death scene that changes the movie.

lead_characters.name: Nadia
lead_characters.demographics: Female, teenager, child/young teen, vulnerable, observant
lead_characters.hook: Nadia is the story's innocence under pressure, a child forced to process adult terror in fragments. Her silence, fear, and small acts of trust give the film a moral stakes layer that keeps the apocalypse from becoming abstract. She is the reason the bunker question never stays philosophical for long.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong young-performer role in the tradition of Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project — emotionally legible, observant, and central to the audience's empathy. It gives a young actor a chance to carry quiet devastation without speeches.

lead_characters.name: Azar
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, father, desperate, likely immigrant or expatriate
lead_characters.hook: Azar is one of the film's clearest faces of panic: a father trying to convert valuables into a future for his family. He is not a villain or a fool, just a man whose bargaining power is evaporating in public. His arc sharpens the film's class and survival themes by showing what the bunker market does to ordinary people.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a painful, grounded turn in the mode of Barkhad Abdi in Captain Phillips or Mahershala Ali in Moonlight's quieter scenes — dignity under pressure. It offers a compact but emotionally loaded portrait of fear.

lead_characters.name: Cyra
lead_characters.hook: Cyra is a parent in triage mode, trying to keep her daughter intact while the world strips away every practical option. She doesn't get speeches, but her presence makes the family's terror feel immediate and real. She helps turn the apocalypse into a domestic crisis, not just a global one.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can land with the quiet force of a Melissa Leo or Frances McDormand supporting turn — a mother whose face tells the story before the dialogue does. It gives an actor a chance to play endurance rather than plot.

lead_characters.name: Victor Reis
lead_characters.hook: Victor is George's uneasy partner and a reminder that even the bunker elite are not fully aligned. He carries the look of a man who has bought into survival as a transaction but is already regretting the price. His presence widens the world of the vault without stealing focus from the central triangle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a useful supporting role for an actor who specializes in compromised authority, like Stanley Tucci in Margin Call or David Strathairn in Good Night, and Good Luck. It offers polished unease and a clear place in the power structure.

lead_characters.name: Elias
lead_characters.hook: Elias is the keeper of the old world, the man who refuses to sell the one record that still means something to him. He gives the script one of its clearest statements about value, memory, and loss: not everything can be monetized without destroying it. He is small in screen time but large in thematic weight.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a veteran actor do a late-career gem in the vein of Richard Jenkins in The Humans or Tom Wilkinson in In the Bedroom — quiet, specific, and emotionally devastating in a few scenes. It gives the performer a single, unforgettable moral stand.

lead_characters.name: Gideon
lead_characters.hook: Gideon is the old-money predator in the room, the kind of man who assumes access and control are the same thing. He is less a character than a social force, a reminder that apocalypse doesn't erase hierarchy — it intensifies it. His confrontation with Marie and Morgan gives the film a sharp class-aggression beat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but juicy antagonist-supporting role in the tradition of John Lithgow in Bombshell or Bruce Dern in Nebraska — a man whose entitlement is the performance. It offers a chance to be instantly legible and instantly hated.

casting_characteristics: one child/young-teen role with significant emotional presence
musical performance ability required for Morgan and Marie
Portuguese-language supporting roles and multilingual dialogue

notable_requirements: Lisbon hotel/bar corridor suite as the primary hub
Lisbon street exteriors during civil-collapse conditions
record store and chocolataria set pieces

technical.vfx_details: Asteroid imagery, broadcast inserts, city-collapse atmosphere, and dream/vision transitions; mostly stylized rather than effects-heavy.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, broken glass, riot aftermath, body handling, and environmental damage dressing.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: prestige theatrical or premium-streaming original with awards-facing positioning.

budget.note: The hotel-bar core keeps the footprint contained, but Lisbon collapse exteriors, night work, asteroid/dream visuals, and repeated crowd scenes will push above a lean indie if not scoped carefully.

casting.note: Morgan and Marie both need musical credibility plus romantic chemistry, and George needs a very specific controlled-menace register; the child role adds another sensitivity point.

development.note: The script is emotionally clear, but the repeated apocalypse-poetry passages and the late reveal structure around the passports, bunker, and song will need disciplined pacing in the room to keep the engine crisp.

comp_set.title: The Last Five Years
comp_set.why_it_comps: A music-driven relationship story where emotional truth is carried through performance and song rather than plot mechanics.

comp_set.title: Melancholia
comp_set.why_it_comps: Apocalypse as emotional pressure-cooker, with the end of the world functioning as a lens on intimacy and dread.

comp_set.title: The Fountain
comp_set.why_it_comps: Lyrical, grief-saturated storytelling that uses visual motifs and romantic longing to carry a metaphysical premise.

comp_set.title: Inside Llewyn Davis
comp_set.why_it_comps: A bruised musician protagonist whose talent, self-sabotage, and melancholy define the entire viewing experience.

comp_set.title: Seeking a Friend for the End of the World
comp_set.why_it_comps: End-of-the-world intimacy with a romantic and bittersweet tone, anchored in human connection rather than spectacle.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who respond to prestige romance, music-driven character drama, and emotionally literate apocalypse stories.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, skewing female but with strong adult-male appeal in the music/character lane; educated, urban, streamer-friendly audience.

budget_tier.note: A contemporary, dialogue-forward feature with one primary hub location, a modest supporting cast, and moderate VFX/atmosphere work.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where emotional sophistication, strong lead performances, and a distinctive visual-music identity matter more than spectacle. The apocalypse hook broadens the pitch, but the real buy is the romantic tragedy and the actor showcase.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is evocative, but the story resolves as a closed emotional arc rather than a franchise or sequel engine.

strengths.what_it_means: That makes the movie easy to pitch and easy to feel: the end of the world is not abstract, it's a pressure test for love, art, and self-worth. Buyers can sell the hook without overselling the spectacle, which is valuable in the prestige lane.
strengths.evidence: The countdown clock, bunker passports, and George's offer are all tied directly to Morgan's need to finish the song and choose who gets saved.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Morgan is a real actor role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead has contradiction, skill, shame, and a visible emotional arc, which is exactly what gives a mid-budget prestige film its casting gravity. This is the kind of part that can attract a serious actor looking for a signature turn.
strengths.evidence: Morgan's cracked watch, unfinished notebook, and late-film choice to reject George's bargain all track a clear internal transformation.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The music motif is story, not decoration.
strengths.what_it_means: Because the song is tied to memory, identity, and survival, the music can function as both emotional engine and marketing asset. That gives the film a recognizable sonic identity and a built-in performance hook.
strengths.evidence: The repeated use of "Stardust," "Waltz for Debby," and Marie's singing of Morgan's lyrics turns the score into plot.

strengths.dimension_or_area: George is a clean, memorable antagonist.
strengths.what_it_means: He gives the film a human face for the system of scarcity, which makes the conflict playable and castable. That kind of elegant villainy is attractive to actors and helps the movie avoid becoming purely atmospheric.
strengths.evidence: George's curated vault, his Polaroids, and his language about buying Morgan and preserving art make him feel like a collector of souls.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The hotel world is highly producible.
strengths.what_it_means: A contained hub with recurring rooms, corridors, and bar spaces gives the film a strong production spine without requiring a sprawling footprint. That helps the script stay in the indie range while still feeling expansive.
strengths.evidence: Most of the story lives in Morgan's room, the bar, the corridor, George's suite, and a few controlled exterior excursions.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Marie gives the film its heartbeat.
strengths.what_it_means: She is not just a love interest; she is the emotional and moral counterweight that keeps the movie from becoming self-pitying. That makes the script more attractive to actresses and gives the audience a second point of identification.
strengths.evidence: Her refusal to be bought, her bond with Nadia, and her rooftop conversations with Morgan all shift the story's moral center.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige, actor-forward apocalypse romance with a clean hook, a contained production footprint, and a genuinely ownable tonal identity. The combination of music, mortality, and class tension gives buyers a film they can position as both intimate and eventful without needing tentpole scale.

items.detail: Several corridor/bar exchanges return to the same Morgan-versus-George and Morgan-versus-time beats in slightly different phrasing. That gives the script atmosphere, but it also means the propulsion is sometimes carried by mood rather than by new information or irreversible turns.

items.area: The music rights are not trivial.
items.detail: "Round Midnight," "Waltz for Debby," and "Ordinary World" are all named and materially important, which means the film is not clearance-light. The music is part of the pitch, but it also creates real budget and legal planning before greenlight.

items.area: Morgan's emotional arc is very interior.
items.detail: The role is strong, but much of the transformation happens through reflection, memory, and private choice rather than external action. That is a virtue in the right lane, but it narrows the audience and makes the film heavily dependent on performance and direction.

items.area: The apocalypse scale stays mostly offscreen.
items.detail: The city collapse is vivid in dialogue and texture, but the film is not built around large-scale disaster set pieces. Buyers looking for visible spectacle will see a contained drama first and a sci-fi event second.

items.area: Marie is compelling but still secondary.
items.detail: She has strong scenes and a clear moral position, but the script remains structurally Morgan's story. That keeps the focus clean, though it also means the film does not fully become a two-hander in the way the chemistry sometimes suggests it could.

issues.headline: The main friction is not concept or tone; it is that the movie asks buyers to trust a very interior, performance-dependent feature with a lot of lyrical repetition. Add in the named-music clearance and the fact that the apocalypse is mostly atmospheric rather than spectacular, and the project becomes a prestige play rather than a broad commercial one.
